# Your First Cast-Iron Skillet Starts Here

**A 10-inch skillet that's ready to cook the moment you unbox it — for $48.**

You've seen cast-iron skillets in restaurant kitchens and on food blogs, and maybe you've thought they looked intimidating. They're not. This skillet arrives pre-seasoned with vegetable oil, so there's no complicated first-time setup. Unwrap it, give it a quick rinse, dry it, and start cooking. That's it.

Cast iron has been a kitchen workhorse for generations because it holds heat steadily, moves from stovetop to oven without missing a beat, and lasts for decades when you treat it right. This one is built to be that skillet for you.

---

## What You'll Love Cooking With It

**Even, steady heat for everyday meals.**
Cast iron retains heat exceptionally well. Whether you're searing a steak, sautéing vegetables, or baking cornbread, the 10-inch cooking surface gives you room to work without crowding the pan.

**From burner to oven in one move.**
Oven-safe to 500°F, so you can start a dish on the stovetop and finish it in the oven — no transferring to another pan.

**Works on your stovetop, whatever kind it is.**
Compatible with gas, electric, ceramic, and induction cooktops. No guesswork about whether it will work in your kitchen.

**Easy pouring, easy lifting.**
Two pour spouts let you drain off drippings or pour a pan sauce cleanly from either side. The long handle gives you a secure grip for everyday maneuvering, and the helper handle on the opposite side gives you a second grip when the skillet is full and you want two hands on it. Both handles are cast iron, which means they're part of the same solid piece — nothing to loosen or break over time.

**A cooking surface that improves as you use it.**
The pre-seasoned vegetable-oil finish gives you a head start. As you cook and care for the skillet, that seasoning builds, and the surface becomes smoother and more release-friendly over time.

---

---

## Care: Simpler Than You Think

Cast iron gets a reputation for high maintenance, but the actual routine takes about a minute.

1. **Wash by hand** with warm water and a brush or sponge. A small amount of mild soap is fine if you need it.
2. **Dry immediately and thoroughly** with a towel. Don't let it air-dry — that's how rust starts.
3. **Wipe a thin layer of oil** over the cooking surface before storing. Any neutral cooking oil works.

That's the whole routine. No special products. No soaking. No scrubbing with steel wool unless something truly stubborn happens.

**Two things to remember:**

- **This skillet is not dishwasher-safe.** The dishwasher will strip the seasoning and promote rust.
- **The handles get hot.** Both the long handle and the helper handle are cast iron and will be hot during and after cooking. Always use oven mitts or a dry towel when handling the skillet.

---

## What You'll Love Cooking With It

**Steady heat that's forgiving while you learn.**
Cast iron holds heat evenly and doesn't swing wildly when you add food to the pan. For a first-time user, that means fewer surprises: less burning in one spot while another stays undercooked, and less need to constantly shuffle food around. You can focus on learning timing and technique instead of fighting hot spots. The 10-inch cooking surface gives you enough room to spread food out without crowding, which helps everything cook more evenly.

**One pan from stovetop to oven — no second dish to figure out.**
Oven-safe to 500°F. As a beginner, this removes a whole category of decisions. You don't need to wonder whether to transfer food to a baking dish or buy a separate pan for finishing. Sear a chicken thigh on the burner, slide the whole skillet into the oven, and it's done. One pan, one less thing to wash, one less step to get wrong.

**Works on whatever stove you already own.**
Compatible with gas, electric, ceramic, and induction cooktops. You don't need to check compatibility lists or worry that your kitchen setup won't work. If you have a stove, this skillet works on it.

**Built-in help for lifting and pouring.**
At 6 pounds, this skillet is heavier than the aluminum pans you may be used to, and that's worth knowing upfront. The long handle gives you a secure grip for everyday lifting and tilting. The helper handle on the opposite side gives you a second grip for when the skillet is full and you want two hands on it — useful when you're still getting a feel for the weight. Both handles are cast iron, so they're part of the same solid piece with nothing to loosen over time. The two pour spouts let you drain drippings or pour a pan sauce cleanly from either side, so you're not trying to tip a heavy pan and hoping for the best.

**The skillet gets easier to work with the more you use it.**
The pre-seasoned vegetable-oil finish gives you a functional surface from day one. As you cook and follow the care routine below, that seasoning builds and the surface becomes smoother and more release-friendly over time. For a beginner, that means the learning curve works in your favor: the skillet rewards practice instead of punishing mistakes.

## What You'll Love Cooking With It

**A real sear on a steak, not a gray, steamed surface.**
When a cold steak hits a thin aluminum pan, the pan's temperature drops and the meat stews in its own moisture instead of browning. Cast iron's weight and density — 6 pounds of it here — hold heat through that contact. The surface stays hot, so you get a deep, browned crust on a steak, a pork chop, or a chicken thigh without needing a restaurant-grade burner. That crust is the flavor difference you've been noticing in restaurant food and wondering why you can't reproduce at home. At $48, this is the tool that closes that gap.

**Crispy skin on chicken without burning it.**
The same heat retention that builds a crust on steak also renders fat slowly and evenly under chicken skin. You get crisp, golden skin without the charred spots that come from a pan that heats unevenly. The 10-inch cooking surface fits two to three chicken thighs without crowding, so each piece gets full contact with the hot surface.

**Start on the stove, finish in the oven, serve from the same pan.**
Oven-safe to 500°F. That means you can sear a frittata on the burner, slide the skillet into the oven to set the eggs, and carry it to the table — no transferring to a baking dish, no extra pan to scrub. Same with cornbread: heat the skillet on the stove, pour in the batter, move it to the oven. The 12-inch rim diameter gives you a wide, stable base that sits securely on a burner and gives you a lip to grip when you're moving the pan with oven mitts.

**Works on whatever stove you already own.**
Compatible with gas, electric, ceramic, and induction cooktops. No compatibility check, no adapter, no guesswork. If you have a stove, this skillet works on it.

**Built-in help for a pan that's heavier than you're used to.**
At 6 pounds, this skillet is noticeably heavier than the aluminum or nonstick pans most beginners are coming from. The long handle gives you a secure one-hand grip for tilting and lifting. The helper handle on the opposite side gives you a second grip when the skillet is loaded and you want two hands — say, when you're moving it from stove to oven. Both handles are cast iron, part of the same solid piece, with nothing to loosen or snap over time. The two pour spouts let you tip off excess fat or pour a pan sauce cleanly from either side, so you're not wrestling a heavy, full pan over the sink.

**The cooking surface gets better the more you cook with it.**
The pre-seasoned vegetable-oil finish gives you a functional surface on day one. Each time you cook and follow the care routine below, that seasoning layer builds. Foods that might stick a little in the first few uses — eggs, for instance — release more easily as the surface matures. The skillet rewards repetition instead of wearing out.
